chunks: And what indicates this interpretation is what informed me —

the Sheikh — may God support him — from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa and from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban — both together — from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Sabbah al-Kinani, from Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him); he said:

I asked him about a man who nods off while he is in salat. He said: "If he does not retain awareness of whether a hadath occurred from him — if it did — then wudu and repetition of the salat are obligatory upon him. But if he is certain that no hadath occurred, then neither wudu nor repetition is required of him."

key_terms.إِعَادَةُ الصَّلَاةِ: repetition of the salat — the obligation to redo the prayer from the beginning
key_terms.حَدَثًا: hadath — a ritual impurity event (e.g., passing wind) that invalidates wudu
key_terms.يَخْفِقُ: to nod off/doze — the drooping of the head in drowsiness during salat, as distinct from full sleep
key_terms.يَسْتَيْقِنُ: to be certain — the state of yaqin (certainty) regarding the absence of hadath

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling in Shia fiqh on nodding off during salat — must one renew wudu and repeat the prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) delivers a legal ruling on brief drowsiness (khafaqa) during salat: if the worshipper cannot remember whether a hadath (ritual impurity event) occurred, wudu and repetition of the salat are mandatory; if he is certain no hadath occurred, neither is required. The ruling enshrines the foundational Shia fiqh principle that yaqin (certainty) overrides doubt in matters of taharah.
